 Laura Beck Thu, October 22, 2026 at 12:00 PM CDT 3 min read EvgeniyShkolenko · Getty Images Every election season, the same question pops up: will this change what I owe? It's fair to wonder, especially when candidates spend months promising tax relief for everyone. So, I asked ChatGPT how the November 3 midterms could hit our tax bills. 
 It turns out, the real stakes are a few years out. Short answer for your next tax return is that it probably won't change at all. The tax rates and deductions for 2026 are already set by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, so the return you file next spring is locked in. What the election shapes is how Congress handles a list of tax breaks that expire starting after 2028.

 What's Already Decided 
 The 2025 tax law made the lower tax brackets permanent and raised the child tax credit to $2,200 per child. Several newer breaks are temporary, though. The deductions for tips, overtime and car loan interest, plus the extra deduction for seniors, are set to expire after 2028. The higher cap on state and local tax deductions runs through 2029. 
 How the Results Could Play Out 
 Analysts see two broad paths. According to ChatGPT, a Republican sweep would likely bring another large tax bill building on the 2025 law, while a divided Congress would more likely mean smaller bipartisan deals or gridlock. Either way, the Congress elected next month serves through January 2029, right when those expiring breaks come due. 
 Lower-Income and Hourly Workers 
 According to the artificial intelligence (AI), tipped and hourly workers have the most riding on the tips and overtime deductions. Candidates from both parties have said they support keeping those cuts, but extending them still requires new legislation. 
 Anyone buying coverage on the ACA marketplace has already felt one change, since the enhanced premium tax credits expired this year. 
 Middle-Income Families and Retirees 
 ChatGPT said that the brackets and the $2,200 child tax credit aren't scheduled to change, so families have less at stake in the near term. 
 Retirees are a different story. The $6,000 senior deduction is one of the breaks expiring after 2028, and its future depends on what this Congress and the next one do. 
 Upper-Middle Earners in High-Tax States 
 The SALT cap sits at $40,400 for 2026 and phases out for incomes above $505,000. Without new action, it falls back to $10,000 in 2030. Homeowners in states with high property and income taxes have the most to gain or lose here. 
 Story Continues High Earners 
 Top earners are mostly watching the overall direction. Their rates are permanent under current law, so a big change would require a new bill. That makes control of Congress the variable to watch. 
 According to the AI, the midterms won't change your next tax return. They will decide who negotiates the tax breaks expiring after 2028, so it pays to know which of those breaks you're counting on today.
